name: Early Dynastic Egypt (Dynasties 1–2)
making_significance: The first two dynasties set royal display in carved palettes, labels and mastaba tombs at Abydos and Saqqara.
materials_techniques: siltstone carving; ivory labels; mudbrick mastabas; early hieroglyphs
functions: rule and display;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: retainers buried with early kings; Nubian A-Group neighbours
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)

name: Old Kingdom dynasties (3–6)
making_significance: Old Kingdom kings organised the quarrying, transport and cutting of stone for the pyramids from Djoser to Pepy II, housing workers in state-supplied towns at Giza.
materials_techniques: limestone and granite quarrying; copper tools; stone sculpture; papyrus logbooks
object_types: pyramids; statues; reliefs; Wadi al-Jarf papyri
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: the work gangs (named in graffiti) and their families; provincial populations; the "slaves built pyramids" myth
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Merer's logbook (Wadi al-Jarf) records limestone transport under Khufu.

name: Middle Kingdom dynasties (11–12)
making_significance: Middle Kingdom courts sponsored fine jewellery, block statues and fortresses in Nubia, and the town of Lahun preserved workers' papyri.
materials_techniques: gold and semi-precious stone jewellery; hard-stone statuary; mudbrick fortification
leaves_out: Nubians under fortress control; Lahun workers

name: Eighteenth Dynasty
other_names: New Kingdom Dynasty 18; Thutmosids and Amarna kings
making_significance: The Eighteenth Dynasty introduced large-scale glassmaking, greatly expanded the Middle Kingdom temple at Karnak, built the Amarna city, and filled royal tombs such as Tutankhamun's.
materials_techniques: glassmaking; faience; gold working; relief carving
object_types: glass vessels; Amarna reliefs; Tutankhamun's burial goods
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Levantine and Nubian captives and tribute-bearers; artisans of Deir el-Medina; the 1922 excavation's colonial politics

name: Ramesside dynasties (19–20)
making_significance: Ramesside kings built Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and the royal tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina staged the earliest known recorded strike (c. 1157 BCE).
materials_techniques: sandstone rock-cutting; relief carving; ostraca writing
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: workers who struck over late rations; the 1960s relocation of Abu Simbel and Nubian villages flooded by the Aswan dam

name: Twenty-fifth (Kushite) Dynasty
other_names: Kushite pharaohs; Napatan dynasty in Egypt
making_significance: The Kushite kings who ruled Egypt revived Old Kingdom forms in statuary and built pyramids at el-Kurru and Nuri.
leaves_out: Egyptological habit of treating Kush as marginal; Nubian present communities

name: Twenty-sixth (Saite) Dynasty
making_significance: Saite rulers commissioned archaizing sculpture and bronzes that deliberately copied Old Kingdom models.
leaves_out: Greek and Carian mercenaries; temple workshops

name: Muhammad Ali dynasty
making_significance: Muhammad Ali and his successors founded state textile mills, the Bulaq press (1820s) and European-style buildings in Cairo, while Egyptian antiquities flowed abroad.
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;record and writing
leaves_out: peasants conscripted to factories and canals; Sudanese enslaved soldiers; antiquities given away

name: Umayyad dynasty
making_significance: The Umayyads built the Dome of the Rock and the Great Mosque of Damascus with Byzantine-trained mosaicists and reformed coinage into purely epigraphic designs (696–97).
materials_techniques: glass mosaic; epigraphic coinage; stone and stucco carving
object_types: Dome of the Rock; coins; desert palaces
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Christian and Jewish majorities and their craftsmen; non-Arab converts (mawali)
notes: Link: Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba (POL).

name: Abbasid dynasty
date_note: to 1258 in Baghdad; shadow caliphs in Cairo to 1517
making_significance: The Abbasid court spread paper-making (Baghdad mill c. 794), developed lustre-painted ceramics at Basra and Samarra and imitated Chinese imports.
materials_techniques: papermaking; lustre glaze; stucco; tin-glaze imitating porcelain
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing;exchange and value
leaves_out: enslaved Zanj labour in southern Iraq (revolt 869–83); Christian and Jewish scribes
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Aghlabid dynasty
making_significance: The Aghlabids rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan and set Iraqi lustre tiles around its mihrab.
materials_techniques: stone and brick building; lustre tiles
leaves_out: Berber populations; Sicily conquered from 827

name: Tulunid dynasty
making_significance: Ahmad ibn Tulun built his Cairo mosque with brick and Samarra-style carved stucco.
leaves_out: Egyptian Coptic majority; Iraqi builders brought from Samarra; enslaved soldiers

name: Buyid dynasty
making_significance: Buyid rulers patronised silver and silks, and a group of "Buyid silks" that surfaced in the 1920s–30s is now largely considered forgery.
leaves_out: the forgers and dealers; genuine Daylamite makers
free_sources: Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ghaznavid dynasty
making_significance: The Ghaznavids built palaces at Lashkari Bazar and Ghazni and carried plunder from raids on Indian temples such as Somnath (1025).
leaves_out: Indian temple communities; enslaved captives; Turkic slave-soldiers

name: Ghurid dynasty
making_significance: The Ghurids raised the Minaret of Jam and their commanders began the Qutb complex in Delhi from reused temple material.
leaves_out: temple builders whose columns were reused; Afghan mountain peoples

name: Great Seljuk dynasty
making_significance: Under Seljuk rule Kashan potters made mina'i and lustre wares and Herat metalworkers inlaid brass with silver and copper.
materials_techniques: mina'i overglaze; lustre; brass inlay; brick vaults
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Persian bureaucrats and makers; Turkmen pastoralists
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Zengid dynasty
making_significance: Nur al-Din commissioned a carved wooden minbar for Jerusalem, installed by Saladin in al-Aqsa in 1187 and destroyed by arson in 1969.
leaves_out: Crusader-held populations; the Aleppan carpenters named on the minbar

name: Ayyubid dynasty
making_significance: Ayyubid Syria produced inlaid brass and enamelled glass, and Saladin's dynasty fortified Cairo and Aleppo.
leaves_out: Crusader states; Coptic and Jewish makers

name: Artuqid dynasty
making_significance: Al-Jazari wrote his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206) for the Artuqid ruler of Diyarbakır.
materials_techniques: automata; water clocks; copper coins with figures
leaves_out: Armenian and Syriac craftsmen; manuscript copyists

name: Rasulid dynasty
making_significance: Yemen's Rasulid sultans ordered inlaid brass and enamelled glass bearing their rosette emblem and compiled scientific almanacs.
functions: rule and display;record and writing;exchange and value
leaves_out: Tihama cultivators; Indian Ocean traders

name: Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu
making_significance: The Turkmen dynasties built the Blue Mosque of Tabriz (1465) and patronised Tabriz manuscript painting before the Safavids.
leaves_out: pastoralist confederates; Armenian subjects

name: Qajar dynasty
making_significance: Qajar shahs commissioned life-size oil portraits, painted lacquer and tiles, and Nasir al-Din Shah took up photography.
materials_techniques: oil painting; papier-mâché lacquer; photography; tiles
leaves_out: women artists; Armenian and Jewish craftsmen; Caucasus territory lost
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Library of Congress (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Pahlavi dynasty
making_significance: The Pahlavi state enforced dress laws (1936 unveiling), industrialised carpets and textiles and founded the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art (1977).
materials_techniques: state textile industry; architecture; museum collecting
leaves_out: women coerced by dress laws; tribal and nomadic weavers; opponents

name: Idrisid dynasty
making_significance: The Idrisids founded Fez, where the Qarawiyyin mosque was established by Fatima al-Fihri in 859.
leaves_out: Amazigh (Berber) populations; Andalusi and Qayrawani settlers

name: Zirid dynasty
making_significance: Zirid Kairouan produced Qur'an manuscripts such as the "Nurse's Qur'an" (1020).
leaves_out: women patrons and scribes; Banu Hilal disruption

name: Almoravid dynasty
making_significance: The Almoravids commissioned the carved and inlaid minbar made in Córdoba (1137) for their Marrakesh mosque.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Saharan and Sahelian peoples; Andalusi artisans

name: Almohad dynasty
making_significance: The Almohads built the Kutubiyya and the Giralda minaret and favoured restrained ornament.
leaves_out: Jews and Christians forced to convert; Amazigh non-Almohad groups

name: Marinid dynasty
making_significance: The Marinids built Fez madrasas with zellij tile mosaic, carved cedar and stucco.
leaves_out: craft guilds of Fez; Jewish quarter (mellah)

name: Hafsid dynasty
making_significance: The Hafsids ruled Tunis, building mosques and madrasas and hosting Andalusi refugee artisans.
leaves_out: Andalusi refugees; Italian captives

name: Saadian dynasty
making_significance: The Saadians built the El Badi palace and the Saadian tombs with wealth from sugar and gold taken after the 1591 invasion of Songhay.
leaves_out: enslaved sugar workers; Songhay conquered

name: Alaouite dynasty
making_significance: Moulay Ismail built Meknes with enslaved and conscripted labour and the dynasty still patronises Moroccan crafts.
leaves_out: enslaved builders and the Abid al-Bukhari army; Amazigh communities

name: Husainid dynasty
making_significance: The Husainid beys built the Bardo palace and commissioned Qallaline tiles.
leaves_out: Tunisian subjects; French protectorate from 1881

name: Zagwe dynasty
making_significance: Tradition credits King Lalibela (r. c. 1181–1221) with the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, though archaeologists date some of the complex earlier.
leaves_out: the church-cutters' names; the "angels built it" tradition

name: Keïta dynasty
making_significance: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage and gold spending made the Keïta rulers known as patrons across the Mediterranean.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: nyamakalaw artisans; enslaved people

name: Askia dynasty
making_significance: Askia Muhammad (r. 1493–1528) built his earthen tomb-pyramid at Gao and backed Timbuktu scholarship after his pilgrimage.
leaves_out: enslaved farming communities; Sorko and Tuareg neighbours; the masons' guilds who maintain the tomb

name: Sayfawa dynasty
making_significance: The Sayfawa ruled Kanem and then Bornu for over seven centuries, one of the longest-lived royal lines, patronising Islamic scholarship and manuscript copying.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: people enslaved and sent north; the Kanembu and Kotoko subjects

name: Mahdali dynasty
making_significance: Mahdali sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman (r. c. 1310–33) built the Husuni Kubwa palace and enlarged the Great Mosque at Kilwa, and the dynasty minted copper coins.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: enslaved people; mainland producers of gold and ivory

name: Oba dynasty of Benin
date_note: c.; traditional start with Eweka I; continues (Oba Ewuare II since 2016)
making_significance: The Obas commissioned brass heads and ivory for royal ancestral altars and the continuing court still claims the objects taken in 1897.
materials_techniques: lost-wax brass; ivory carving; coral beadwork
leaves_out: guild members as makers; the Edo state's and Nigerian federal claims in restitution debates
free_sources: Digital Benin (open data);Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)
notes: Link: Kingdom of Benin (POL); the dynasty outlives the kingdom's 1897 conquest.

name: Oyoko royal line of Asante
making_significance: The Asantehene's court remains the patron of regalia, stools and gold ornaments and has borrowed back objects taken by Britain.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: makers' guild villages (e.g. Bonwire weavers, Ahwiaa carvers); chiefs outside the royal clan

name: Satavahana dynasty
making_significance: Under Satavahana rule, donors including ivory-workers of Vidisha funded the carved gateways of Sanchi and stupas such as Amaravati.
materials_techniques: sandstone and limestone relief; rock-cut caves
object_types: Sanchi gateways; Amaravati reliefs; Karle chaitya
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: the guilds and donors who actually paid (named in inscriptions); Amaravati marbles dispersed to London and Chennai
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)

name: Vakataka dynasty
making_significance: Under the Vakataka king Harishena (c. 460–480), courtiers funded the later painted caves of Ajanta.
leaves_out: painters and monks; 19th-c. copying and damage

name: Pallava dynasty
making_significance: The Pallavas carved the monolithic rathas and relief of Mamallapuram and built the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, whose script spread to Southeast Asia.
materials_techniques: granite rock-cutting; structural temples; Pallava Grantha script
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: sculptors and quarrymen; Chalukya rivals

name: Chalukya dynasty of Badami
making_significance: The Badami Chalukyas cut cave temples at Badami and built experimental temples at Aihole and Pattadakal.
leaves_out: named architects (inscriptions at Pattadakal); Pallava rivals

name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
making_significance: Under Krishna I the Rashtrakutas had the Kailasa temple (Ellora Cave 16) carved from a single hillside.
leaves_out: the unrecorded carvers; Buddhist and Jain caves alongside

name: Chandela dynasty
making_significance: The Chandelas built the sandstone temples of Khajuraho with dense figural sculpture around 950–1050.
leaves_out: sculptors' guilds; colonial prudishness in interpretation

name: Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty
making_significance: The Solanki court built the Modhera Sun Temple (1026) and Queen Udayamati's stepwell Rani ki Vav.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;food and storage
leaves_out: Jain merchant patrons; Somnath raid

name: Hoysala dynasty
making_significance: Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were carved in soapstone by sculptors who signed their work.
leaves_out: women dancers depicted; Delhi Sultanate sack
notes: Signed works (e.g. Mallitamma) make Hoysala a case for F1.26.

name: Eastern Ganga dynasty
making_significance: Eastern Ganga kings built the Jagannath temple at Puri and the Konark Sun Temple (c. 1250).
leaves_out: temple workers; Odia present communities

name: Kakatiya dynasty
making_significance: The Kakatiyas built the Warangal gateways and the Ramappa temple (1213) with lightweight bricks.
leaves_out: the Koh-i-Noor's claimed origin

name: Sena dynasty
making_significance: The Senas continued Bengal's black-stone sculpture for Hindu cults after the Palas.
leaves_out: Buddhist institutions in decline

name: Khalji dynasty
making_significance: Alauddin Khalji built the Alai Darwaza (1311) with true arches and red sandstone and marble inlay.
leaves_out: raided southern kingdoms; Mongol captives

name: Tughluq dynasty
making_significance: Firoz Shah Tughluq moved Ashokan pillars to Delhi and his predecessors built the sloping walls of Tughlaqabad.
leaves_out: populations moved to Daulatabad; enslaved labour
notes: Pillar relocation is a reuse case.

name: Adil Shahi dynasty
making_significance: The Adil Shahis built the Gol Gumbaz and Ibrahim II patronised a distinctive Bijapur painting.
leaves_out: Habshi (African) nobles and soldiers; Mughal conquest

name: Qutb Shahi dynasty
making_significance: The Qutb Shahis built the Charminar (1591) and ruled the diamond and painted-cotton trade of Masulipatnam.
leaves_out: diamond miners; weavers

name: Nayaka dynasty of Madurai
making_significance: The Madurai Nayakas enlarged the Meenakshi temple with towering gopurams and pillared halls.
leaves_out: temple servants; Tamil Muslim traders

name: Wodeyar dynasty
making_significance: The Wodeyars patronised Mysore painting and the Dasara festival and built the Mysore Palace (1912).
leaves_out: artisans of palace workshops

name: Sisodia dynasty of Mewar
making_significance: The Sisodias kept a court painting workshop at Udaipur producing large festival paintings.
leaves_out: named and unnamed court painters; Bhil communities

name: Kachhwaha dynasty
making_significance: Jai Singh II founded Jaipur (1727) with astronomical instruments (Jantar Mantar) and a painting workshop.
leaves_out: artisan communities settled by caste-based quarters in Jaipur; Mina communities displaced from Amber

name: Malla dynasty (Nepal)
making_significance: The Malla kings of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur commissioned Newar copper casting, woodcarving and Durbar Square temples.
leaves_out: Newar artisan castes (Shakya, Tamrakar); Gorkha conquest
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Himalayan Art Resources (link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Namgyal dynasty (Ladakh)
making_significance: The Namgyal kings built Leh Palace and supported Hemis monastery.
leaves_out: Balti and Muslim neighbours

name: Sailendra dynasty
making_significance: The Sailendra kings sponsored Borobudur in Central Java, the largest Buddhist monument, carved with 2,672 relief panels.
leaves_out: corvée labourers and carvers; the Sanjaya line and Hindu contemporaries; heads removed from Borobudur Buddhas for collections

name: Trần dynasty
making_significance: The Trần court repelled Mongol invasions and patronised the Trúc Lâm Zen school and ceramics.
leaves_out: Cham neighbours

name: Later Lê dynasty
making_significance: The Lê period saw Chu Đậu blue-and-white exports and doctoral stelae at the Temple of Literature.
leaves_out: Cham; Mạc usurpers

name: Nguyễn dynasty
making_significance: The Nguyễn built the Huế citadel and tombs and ordered "Bleu de Huế" porcelain from China.
leaves_out: French protectorate after 1883

name: Konbaung dynasty
making_significance: The Konbaung court built Mandalay and its regalia was taken by Britain in 1885.
leaves_out: regalia partly returned 1964

name: Chakri dynasty
making_significance: The Chakri kings built Bangkok's Grand Palace and dress the Emerald Buddha seasonally.
leaves_out: Lao and Khmer war captives settled as labour; the Emerald Buddha taken from Vientiane in 1779; artisans of the royal craft departments

name: Imperial house of Japan
date_note: c.; historically attested from about the 6th century; continues
making_significance: The imperial house's Shōsōin repository has preserved 8th-century objects since 756, and from 1890 the Imperial Household named master craftspeople as Imperial Household Artists.
leaves_out: restricted access to imperial tombs (kofun) for archaeology; commoner makers
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Fujiwara regents
making_significance: Fujiwara no Yorimichi built the Byōdōin Phoenix Hall (1053) and commissioned the sculptor Jōchō's joined-wood Amida.
leaves_out: estate cultivators who funded the court; Jōchō's workshop assistants
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ashikaga shoguns
making_significance: The Ashikaga shoguns built Kinkaku-ji and Ginkaku-ji and ranked imported Chinese objects (karamono) with the help of connoisseurs such as Nōami.
defined_by: historians; the Kundaikan sōchōki connoisseurship manual
leaves_out: dōbōshū attendants (often of low status) who shaped taste; Chinese and Korean makers
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Toyotomi
making_significance: Hideyoshi built a portable golden tea room and his invasions of Korea (1592–98) took Korean potters to Japan, founding new kilns.
leaves_out: abducted Korean potters; Korean casualties; tea master Sen no Rikyū (ordered to die 1591)
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Tokugawa shoguns
making_significance: The Tokugawa shoguns built the Nikkō Tōshōgū mausoleum and retained Kanō-school painters as official artists, setting a court taste copied by daimyo.
materials_techniques: lacquer; polychrome carving; painting on screens
leaves_out: carpenters, carvers and painters; daimyo made to fund construction; townspeople's own art market (ukiyo-e)
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Maeda clan of Kaga
making_significance: The Maeda lords of Kaga ran a domain craft workshop (saikusho) and fostered Kaga maki-e, Kutani porcelain and dyeing.
leaves_out: domain artisans and commoner workshops; later Kutani revival makers
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Nabeshima clan of Saga
making_significance: The Nabeshima brought Korean potters after the 1590s invasions, whose discovery of porcelain clay near Arita began Japanese porcelain, and ran the Ōkawachi kilns for Nabeshima ware.
leaves_out: Korean potters (e.g. Yi Sam-pyeong/Ri Sanpei)
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Chinggisid lineage
date_note: c.; last Chinggisid khans in the Kazakh steppe
making_significance: Descent from Chinggis Khan legitimised khans from the Yuan and Ilkhanate to Crimea and the Kazakh hordes, and so shaped who could commission court art for six centuries.
leaves_out: non-Chinggisid rulers who had to rule through puppet khans (Timur)

name: Shaybanid dynasty
making_significance: The Shaybanids ruled Bukhara and Samarkand, patronising madrasas and a Bukhara school of manuscript painting.
leaves_out: Herat painters taken to Bukhara; Persian captives

name: Julio-Claudian dynasty
making_significance: Augustus and his successors fixed an official classicising style in the Ara Pacis, standard portrait types copied across the empire, and court cameos such as the Gemma Augustea.
materials_techniques: marble relief; portrait copying; cameo cutting; cast glass
leaves_out: enslaved and freed workshop labour; provincial copyists; conquered Egypt's treasury
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Getty Museum Open Content (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons

name: Macedonian dynasty (Byzantine)
making_significance: Macedonian emperors presided over a revival of classical models in manuscripts such as the Paris Psalter and in carved ivory triptychs and caskets.
materials_techniques: ivory carving; manuscript illumination; cloisonné enamel
defined_by: historians; the term "Macedonian Renaissance" is modern
leaves_out: Bulgarians conquered by Basil II; imperial silk workers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Palaiologan dynasty
making_significance: Under the Palaiologoi the statesman Theodore Metochites funded the Chora church mosaics and frescoes (1315–21), and micro-mosaic icons were made in Constantinople.
leaves_out: a shrinking empire's peasants; Latin and Ottoman neighbours

name: Merovingian dynasty
making_significance: Merovingian rulers wore gold and garnet cloisonné, like the bees from Childeric's grave, found in 1653 and mostly stolen from Paris in 1831.
leaves_out: Gallo-Roman makers; the stolen grave goods

name: Ottonian dynasty
making_significance: Ottonian emperors and bishops commissioned illuminated manuscripts at Reichenau and cast bronze doors such as Bernward's at Hildesheim (1015).
leaves_out: monastic scribes and painters; Slavic peoples east of the Elbe

name: Hohenstaufen dynasty
making_significance: Frederick II built Castel del Monte, struck gold augustales in a Roman manner and wrote a treatise on falconry.
materials_techniques: gold coinage; castle building; manuscript illustration
leaves_out: Muslims deported to Lucera; Italian communes

name: Hauteville dynasty
date_note: Norman siege of Palermo 1071, city taken January 1072; kingdom from 1130
making_significance: Roger II's Palermo combined Byzantine mosaics, a painted muqarnas ceiling in the Fatimid manner and a silk coronation mantle with an Arabic inscription (1133–34).
materials_techniques: mosaic; painted muqarnas; silk and pearl embroidery
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Muslim and Greek makers who were later expelled or assimilated

name: Capetian dynasty
making_significance: Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle for relics, and Paris craft statutes were compiled in Étienne Boileau's Livre des métiers (c. 1268).
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: Jews expelled 1306; women in trades (some guilds were women's)

name: Valois dynasty
making_significance: Valois kings and princes commissioned books of hours such as the Très Riches Heures and Francis I's Fontainebleau with Italian artists.
leaves_out: Huguenot artisans; peasant costs of war

name: Bourbon dynasty
date_note: France 1589–1792 and 1814–30; branches in Spain and Naples
making_significance: Louis XIV's Versailles was furnished by the Gobelins manufactory, and Louis XV made Sèvres a royal porcelain works.
leaves_out: enslaved people in French colonies; workers at royal manufactures
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Getty Museum Open Content (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons

name: Tudor dynasty
making_significance: Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries (1536–41) destroyed and dispersed religious art while Holbein painted the court.
leaves_out: monastic makers and communities; Catholic and Irish subjects
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;National Gallery of Art Washington (CC0)

name: Habsburg dynasty
making_significance: Habsburg Kunstkammern such as Ambras and Rudolf II's Prague collected objects from across the empire, including the feather headdress in Vienna associated with Moctezuma.
leaves_out: colonised peoples whose objects were collected; Mexico's request for the headdress

name: Medici
date_note: as patrons from Cosimo il Vecchio; grand dukes from 1569
making_significance: The Medici commissioned art, founded a pietre dure workshop (1588) and, through Anna Maria Luisa's 1737 Family Pact, kept their collections in Florence.
materials_techniques: pietre dure; bronze casting; painting; early porcelain
object_types: collections; pietre dure tables; Medici porcelain
leaves_out: artisans and guild workers; women patrons

name: Gonzaga
making_significance: The Gonzaga of Mantua commissioned Mantegna's Camera degli Sposi and sold much of their collection to Charles I of England in 1627–28.
leaves_out: Isabella d'Este's role as patron

name: Wettin dynasty (Albertine Saxony)
making_significance: Augustus the Strong founded Meissen, Europe's first hard-paste porcelain works (1710), and the Green Vault treasury.
leaves_out: Böttger and Tschirnhaus's workers; Chinese and Japanese models copied

name: Romanov dynasty
making_significance: The Romanovs patronised the Imperial Porcelain Factory (1744) and ordered Fabergé eggs as Easter gifts.
leaves_out: serfs; Siberian fur tributaries

name: Jagiellonian dynasty
making_significance: Sigismund II Augustus commissioned Flemish tapestries for Wawel, which were evacuated in 1939 and returned from Canada in 1961.
leaves_out: Flemish weavers; Lithuanian and Ruthenian subjects

name: Nemanjić dynasty
making_significance: The Nemanjić rulers founded monasteries with frescoes such as Studenica, Mileševa and Sopoćani.
leaves_out: peasants; Greek painters employed

name: Hohenzollern dynasty
making_significance: Frederick II made the Berlin porcelain works royal (KPM, 1763), and Prussia's 1813 "gold for iron" campaign swapped jewellery for cast-iron pieces.
leaves_out: Polish subjects; industrial workers

name: Kalākaua dynasty
